narrative: The model estimated an 88.3% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt, and that high risk is why your law school application was rejected. This is not a judgment that you cannot succeed; it means the information reviewed placed you well outside the pattern of students who passed. Gender and race were not part of this prediction. The strongest factor was your third-year class standing: you are in the lowest decile, while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile. Your first-year standing was the second-most influential factor and pointed the same way—you were also in the lowest decile, compared with an accepted average near the sixth decile. Together, these academic-standing signals substantially pushed the prediction toward failure. Your undergraduate GPA was the third-most important factor and its influence was slightly toward passing, but at 2.90 it was still below the accepted-student average of 3.23, so it did not offset the concern about your law-school standing. To improve a future application, focus on evidence that you can handle bar-level material: meet with an academic advisor, consider additional coursework or a structured bar-readiness program, prepare for a stronger LSAT if you retake it, and be ready to explain any circumstances behind your early class standing. A later application should show sustained academic improvement and a realistic study plan.
